The exercise asks:

> Exercise 4 (8 pts). For which values of k does the system x+y+kz=1, x+ky+z=1, kx+y+z=1 have unique, infinite or no solutions?

Start by writing the coefficients of $x$, $y$, and $z$ as a matrix:

$$
A =
\begin{pmatrix}
1 & 1 & k \\
1 & k & 1 \\
k & 1 & 1
\end{pmatrix}
$$

For a square system, if $\det(A) \ne 0$, there is a unique solution. If $\det(A)=0$, the system has no unique solution, so you then check whether it is consistent to distinguish infinitely many solutions from none.

To get started, expand $\det(A)$ along the first row. The signs are $+,-,+$. The first term uses the $2 \times 2$ minor left after deleting the first row and first column.

Calculate that first minor’s determinant: $\begin{vmatrix} k & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{vmatrix}$.
Ok so I write the coefficient matrix and take its determinant? I got det = k³ − 3k + 2.

content:
The exercise is:

> Exercise 4 (8 pts). For which values of $k$ does the system $x+y+kz=1,\ x+ky+z=1,\ kx+y+z=1$ have unique, infinite or no solutions?

Write the system as $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$, where $A$ contains the coefficients, $\mathbf{x}$ contains the unknowns, and $\mathbf{b}$ contains the right-hand sides.

A **unique solution** means there is exactly one vector $\mathbf{x}$ that satisfies all three equations.

If $\det(A)\ne 0$, the columns of $A$ are independent, so $A$ has an inverse. Multiplying both sides by that inverse gives one determined value of $\mathbf{x}$. That is why the system has a unique solution.

If $\det(A)=0$, the columns are dependent: there is a nonzero vector $\mathbf{u}$ with $A\mathbf{u}=\mathbf{0}$. If $\mathbf{x}_0$ is one solution, then for any number $t$,

$$
A(\mathbf{x}_0+t\mathbf{u})
= A\mathbf{x}_0+tA\mathbf{u}
= \mathbf{b}+t\mathbf{0}
= \mathbf{b}.
$$

So every $\mathbf{x}_0+t\mathbf{u}$ is also a solution. There cannot be exactly one: either the system has no solution, or it has infinitely many.

For this exercise, $\det(A)=0$ only tells you that the solution is not unique; you still need to check whether the equations are consistent to distinguish infinitely many solutions from none.

In your own words, what happens to the solutions when a nonzero vector $\mathbf{u}$ satisfies $A\mathbf{u}=\mathbf{0}$?

issues.where: “Rewrite the given system as $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$, and tell me what $\mathbf{b}$ is.”
issues.fix: This repeats the setup the student has already done and does not directly address why determinant zero rules out a unique solution. End by asking them to explain, in their own words, what happens to solutions when a nonzero vector $\mathbf{u}$ satisfies $A\mathbf{u}=\mathbf{0}$.
